scanRules.matching: A scanner lowercases the item text (vignette, stem, options, rationale) and checks each keyword as a whole word or phrase (word boundaries, not inside other words). severity 'high': one keyword hit flags the item. severity 'medium' or 'low': at least 2 different keywords of the same entry must hit.
scanRules.onHit: A flagged item must be fixed according to the entry guidance, or carry a visible 'check textbook' flag. 'do not use' means rewrite so the item does not depend on the claim at all.
scanRules.neverDo: Do not replace a doubtful claim by a fact from memory. Where the correction is unsure, the item must stay silent on it and say 'verify in current textbook/official source'.
scanRules.caveat: Keywords are heuristics. A hit is a reason to look, not proof of an error. All preset notes are AI-written and not nurse-reviewed.

entries.claim: The preset note cites RA 6173 for the public officials code of conduct; the note itself says this is probably RA 6713. Verify in current textbook/official source; never put either number in a stem or key.
The handout writes 'E0 2009' for the Family Code; probably Executive Order 209. Verify in current textbook/official source before any item names it.
The source material mixed up RA 10352 and RA 10351. Do not write items that depend on either number or on which law it names; verify in current textbook/official source.
AO 2007-0012 is superseded in the source material. Do not use it as a current policy; verify in current textbook/official source.
EO 352 was left unresolved (unclear what it covers or whether it is current). Do not use; verify in current textbook/official source.
One drug name on handout page 101 could not be read. Do not write items about any drug whose name was reconstructed from that page; verify in current textbook/official source.

The handout antidote table does not cover cyanide and the antidote list is dated in places. Verify in current textbook/official source; ask about airway and breathing priority rather than the antidote.

Antidote and management for tricyclic overdose is not reliably given in the handout and older teaching may be outdated. Verify in current textbook/official source; ask about monitoring and airway priority.
The handout lists acetylcysteine only as a use, not as a full antidote protocol, and regimens differ by source. Verify in current textbook/official source; no doses or protocol timing in items.
Antidote pairs come from one handout list. Phentolamine for MAOI crisis is listed there but not standard everywhere. Verify pairs in current textbook/official source; avoid reversal doses.
The handout digoxin range reads like a unit slip. Do not state a range or unit; ask about recognising toxicity and holding the drug instead.

HIV cause and transmission text is missing from the communicable disease handout, so the note rests on general knowledge, and an older line on breastfeeding in AIDS is outdated per the nutrition note. Verify in current textbook/official source; avoid current national policy claims.
The antidiabetic drug section is missing from the pharmacology handout, so drug lists and cautions in the notes rest on general knowledge. Verify in current textbook/official source; no doses.

The handout states the Standard Days Method cannot be used with cycles of 26 to 32 days, which the note flags as reversed. The fertile-day window is standard teaching, not from the handout. Verify in current textbook/official source before using any cycle length or day range.

keywords: rule of nines for a child
entries.claim: The handout child percentages look garbled (they should add to about 100 and the trunk split is unclear). Avoid child body-surface percentages; ask about priority (airway, fluids, burn centre referral) instead; verify in current textbook/official source.
Adult Rule of Nines is standard teaching but regional percentages differ in some sources. Flag check textbook if an item depends on a specific percentage.
Calorie and protein targets for burns in the handout are very high and unconfirmed. Do not state numbers; ask whether a high-calorie, high-protein diet is indicated.
Fluid formulas, volumes, urine output targets and colloid timing differ by source. Avoid numbers; ask which phase or which priority comes first.
The handout says sodium is low in both emergent and acute phases, and phase names and timing vary by book. Flag check textbook.
The handout equates first degree with superficial partial thickness and second with deep partial, unlike many books. Use one consistent term set and flag check textbook.
The handout calls silver sulfadiazine most bactericidal and gives a doubtful TBSA limit for mafenide. Flag check textbook; no concentrations or limits.
The handout beer allowance for MAOI diets is doubtful. Ask which foods to avoid in general, never an allowed quantity; verify in current textbook/official source.

Lithium target ranges differ between books and the handout salt-intake line is a typo. Do not give a numeric range; ask about the priority action when toxicity signs appear or when to draw the level. Verify in current textbook/official source.
Handout says 'salt intake 2-3 L/day' (clear typo) and mannitol for toxicity is not standard in most sources. Ask only that sodium and fluid intake stay steady.
NP1-NP5 area labels and TOS weights in the notes and prompts are unofficial, from second-hand summaries; exam weighting is UNKNOWN. Never state percentages or claim what the board 'tests most'.
The handout lists both gluteal sites without comment; newer guidance often prefers ventrogluteal. Avoid items that depend on which site is 'best'.
Which infant dose rule a school expects differs; the handout gives Fried's rule in months. Avoid rule-based answers; calc items must supply their own formula.
The handout labels dextrose-in-saline mixes hypertonic; D5W is isotonic in the bag but acts like free water. Flag check textbook; avoid classification-only items.
The handout gives only left side lying for air embolism; many books add Trendelenburg. Ask for the first nursing action, not the exact position.
The handout lists nearly every agent as killing everything, which is oversimplified (for example alcohol does not kill spores). Do not write 'kills all' statements.
Disease groupings under droplet, airborne and contact precautions differ between texts (e.g. hepatitis A, rubella, chickenpox). Use clear-cut examples only.
Color schemes differ between agencies and the handout version may not match the DOH regulation. Avoid bag-color questions; verify in current textbook/official source.
Oxygen delivery percentages are estimates and one handout figure was misread. Ask about device choice or priority, not the exact FiO2 or flow.
Auscultation of injected air is no longer considered reliable alone (X-ray is the gold standard) and head positioning teaching differs. Flag check textbook.
Retention time ('13 hours') is probably wrong and the handout gives the same details for different solutions. Avoid times and volumes; ask about safety (children, kidney clients).
The handout oliguria threshold reads 'greater than 30 ml/hr', almost certainly a typo for less than. Ask about the nursing action for low urine output, not the cut-off.
The handout does not give timing of each reaction or drug names. Ask about the first action (stop the transfusion, keep line open, notify), not timing or doses.
The handout pediatric site is unusual and lists older disease terms and cell patterns. Flag check textbook.
The handout contradicts itself on whether a revoked license can be reissued (permanent versus after four years). Do not write items on this; verify in current textbook/official source.
The 30-day appeal period, the Section 15 citation and what the law repealed need confirmation. Avoid periods and section numbers.
The RA 2382 line in the handout has stray text copied from the RA 3573 line and a duplicate RA 9211 entry. Do not use; verify in current textbook/official source.
PD 996 is quoted with children 'below 8 years'; the age needs confirmation. Do not use the age or the decree number; verify in current textbook/official source.
Law numbers and years in the preset notes come from handouts and memory and are unverified. Ask what a law covers, never its number or year; verify in current textbook/official source.
The elderly discount law may have been amended since the handout (which gives 20%). Avoid discount percentages and law numbers.
Age cut-offs (9 years; below 18; above 70) come from the handout and Philippine law has been amended on minors. Do not state ages; verify in current textbook/official source.

Local rules for minors, sterilization consent, refusal of care and DNR signers are not in the handout. Ask about the principle (autonomy, who can consent), not legal procedure; verify in current textbook/official source.
The handout staffing table is garbled; rounding and the 365-day convention depend on the instructor. Calc items must supply every number and the method.
Hospital-type ratios in the handout appear as garbled text read as 55:45, 60:40. Avoid ratios; verify in the DOH manual.
Scope for practical nurses and aides varies by agency and law. Ask about the delegation principle (stable, predictable tasks; the nurse keeps accountability), not named local rules.

Books name and group COPAR phases and principles differently (the handout puts SALT and core-group formation in the entry phase). Ask about order or purpose only when phase groupings agree; flag check textbook.
DOH vision, mission, number of functions, structure, attached agencies and reorganization/devolution laws change over time. Avoid; verify in current textbook/official source.
The numeric weights of the family health problem prioritization scale are not confirmed even by the note author. Avoid weights; ask about relative priority.
Books group health promotion, specific protection, prompt treatment and disability limitation under different levels. Use only unambiguous examples.
Philippine anti-smoking provisions and public-program medicines are not confirmed in the note. Avoid provisions; verify in current textbook/official source.
The handout calls lepromatous leprosy both 'not infectious' and 'infectious'; the multibacillary type is the infectious one. Keep to that wording; flag check textbook.
Wound-washing time and the animal-bite vaccine schedule are unconfirmed. Ask about the first action, not minutes or schedule.
Multipliers, rate versus ratio wording and dependency-ratio age cut-offs differ by text. Calc items must supply the formula and multiplier.

The immunization schedule, vaccine list, dose pattern and fully-immunized definition in the handout are older than current national schedules. Ask about contraindications or nursing actions, not ages, intervals or dose counts; verify in current textbook/official source.
Temperature ranges, shelf placement, carrier hold time and the open-vial policy are from general training, not the handout. Avoid numbers.

The handout prenatal-visit pattern is older than DOH guidance, vitamin A in pregnancy is now handled cautiously, and IMCI cut-offs are unconfirmed. Ask about priority classification, not counts or cut-offs.
Methods the DOH provides, pill and injectable schedules and the day-count rules are unconfirmed. Avoid schedules and day counts.
Dose intervals, protection percentages, Td replacing TT and the adult booster rule are unconfirmed. Avoid intervals and percentages.
Timing of cord clamping (handout differs from 1 to 3 minutes taught elsewhere), vitamin K, vaccines, bath delay and oxytocin dose vary. Ask about the sequence principle, not minutes or doses.
The collection window, number of disorders in the panel and the hearing-screening law are unconfirmed. Avoid hours and disorder counts.
The handout has no VAWC section; provisions, order durations and mandatory reporting duties are unconfirmed. Ask about the nursing response (safety, documentation), not legal durations.
The endorsed herb list, uses and age-based preparation amounts are unconfirmed. Avoid amounts; flag check textbook.
Supplement schedules, fortification list and stunting/wasting cut-offs were not in the handout, and the 'no breastfeeding in AIDS' line is outdated. Avoid doses, cut-offs and current policy.
Household counts, safe distances, boiling and chlorine amounts, and toilet-level grouping vary. Avoid numbers.
The handout cold-holding limit is higher than the commonly taught one; rating classes and permit issuer are unconfirmed. Avoid temperatures.
The handout says LH peaks in the luteal phase; textbooks place the LH surge just before ovulation. Day ranges vary. Avoid day counts.
The handout definition of nulliparous is muddled and gives term as 38-42 weeks (usually 37-42). Avoid week boundaries; flag check textbook.

The handout gives overlapping or inconsistent age bands for stages (preschool 3-5 and 4-6; school-age 6-12 and 7-12; formal operations 11 or 12). Ask what a child at a stage can do, not boundary ages.
The handout starts the 'poor' band at 1 rather than 0. Avoid cut-off scores; ask about the next action.

For these anomalies the handout lacks repair timing, post-op care or treatment (the Ponseti method is not named; the cremasteric reflex nerve level differs). Ask about recognition and safety priorities; avoid timing and surgical details.
The handout gives no definitions, murmurs, treatment or timing for these defects. Avoid surgery names and drug doses (including PGE1).
Digoxin hold parameters for infants and fluid guidance are not in the handout. Ask about the priority action; no hold numbers.
The handout puts the apical impulse at the '15th' intercostal space (typo; the note says adult apex is 5th ICS, left mid-clavicular). Flag check textbook if location is asked.
The handout exercise cardiac-output figure ('fourfold to 2 L/min') cannot be right. Avoid numbers.
The handout AV delay ('0.8 milliseconds') and T-wave limit look garbled; QT varies with heart rate. Avoid interval and amplitude values.
Dosing and hold parameters are not in the handout. Ask about monitoring or priority, not values.
Indomethacin guidance from the handout differs from some references, and opioid use in pleurisy needs a drug-book check.
Number of doses, spacing, storage and interactions are not in the handout. Ask about the priority action; no tablet counts or timing.
Modern guidelines treat morphine and oxygen more selectively than the older MONA approach (oxygen mainly when saturation is low). Ask about priority, not the full MONA list.
Hypertension thresholds differ between guidelines (some use 130/80). Do not ask for a cut-off; ask about priority actions for a hypertensive crisis or a client reading.
The handout calls beta-blockers first line; modern guidance generally favours other classes. Do not ask 'first-line' questions.
The handout applies warm moist packs; some references limit local heat. Do not ask about heat; the no-massage rule is standard teaching.
The handout is unclear on panlobular details and blurs which type gives which signs. Avoid bloater/puffer matching; the low-flow oxygen reason is standard teaching.
The handout describes a Valsalva-type breath during dressing; common teaching is a dressing taped on three sides. Observation size thresholds also vary. Ask about priority, not dressing technique.

TB doses, the 8-week/4-7 month schedule and food advice are from the handout and may differ from the DOH program; the class system is the older American one. No doses, durations or categories; verify in current textbook/official source.
Drug-effect pairs are standard teaching but rifampin food advice and program regimens differ. Flag check textbook.
The handout does not say which lab goes with which anticoagulant. The pairing of aPTT with heparin and PT/INR with warfarin is standard teaching; avoid target ranges, diet rules and doses.
The handout lists Z-track parenteral iron under pernicious anemia; that belongs to iron deficiency anemia. The Schilling test is rarely used today.
Technique names, example sentences and whether 'voicing doubt' is acceptable differ by book. Prefer clear-cut communication choices.
Phase names (handout versus the older Peplau names) and which tasks sit in which phase differ by book. Avoid phase-assignment items.
Crisis duration and phase counts differ among books and the third crisis type is named differently. Avoid durations and counts.
Order durations, face-to-face evaluation and renewal come from law and facility policy, not the handout. Ask for least restrictive first and the priority action; no time limits.

The handout calls SSRIs the safest drug during a panic attack (they act slowly) and advises anxiolytics before meals; both are doubtful. Do not write items on these; verify in current textbook/official source.
Handout says panic attacks last 15 to 30 minutes; many books say they peak within about 10 minutes. Avoid durations.

keywords: once a week for three months
entries.claim: Weight cut-offs, bulimia frequency, refeeding steps and drug choices in the handout are dated. Avoid numbers and drug-choice items.
The handout lists dialysis and lavage for intoxication (extreme cases only) and gives no reliable timeline. Avoid timelines and drug choices; ask about airway and safety first.

The handout calls naltrexone a drug for overdose, which is naloxone's job; naltrexone blocks effects and reduces craving. Propoxyphene, normethadone and levomethadyl are rarely available now. No dosing; verify in current textbook/official source.
Handout white-cell schedule for clozapine may be out of date and 'take after meals' is not firm. Ask about the priority action when signs appear; no schedules.
Handout treats mixed episode and rapid cycling as the same; rapid cycling usually means 4 or more episodes in a year. Avoid duration and episode-count criteria.

The handout lists mirtazapine, maprotiline and amoxapine among tricyclics and calls TCAs 'first choice' then says SSRIs replaced them; the bupropion seizure figure is unverified. Use SSRIs as first line only when explicit; avoid class-membership edge cases.
The handout voltage ('70-50 volts') looks garbled and indications such as schizophrenia and mania vary by source. Avoid electrical values; ask about pre- and post-procedure priorities.
IQ bands and labels vary by manual (newer ones grade by adaptive function), pemoline is withdrawn in many countries and the ADHD onset age wording changed. Avoid IQ numbers and drug-specific items.
Category names, colours, target times, ESI resource lists and danger-zone vitals vary by scale and age; no handout covers these. Ask which client is seen first; avoid colour/time/cut-off facts.
What PENA stands for and its levels are UNKNOWN. Do not write items about it.
Some references place catastrophic bleeding first (C-ABC); where oxygen and IV access sit differs by book. Use the airway-breathing-circulation priority only where the stem makes the context clear.

No handout covers resuscitation or choking; rates, depth, ratio, shock energy, drug doses and child/infant sequences must be verified against current guidelines. Ask about the first action, not numbers.
Gas values, oxygen targets for chronic lung disease and ventilator settings need current guidelines. Ask about priority; no values.
Books differ on listing obstructive shock separately and on stage names; the handout ties septic shock to gram-negative infection only. Avoid classification edge cases.
Fluid volumes, targets, tourniquet protocols and whether legs are raised 20 degrees or flat differ. Avoid numbers; ask about the first action.
Exact GCS component scores and thresholds differ by source (the handout also mentions GCS-P); glucose in an unconscious client needs an order. Avoid score cut-offs.
Sepsis definitions have changed over time; DIC lab values, product choice, heparin use and ICU pressure ranges are not in handouts. Avoid definitions, values and bundle timing.
Decree and law numbers come from handouts and memory; the number and names of disaster phases differ (three to five); council membership and agency roles change. Avoid numbers and phase counts.
Philippine emergency-care and deposit laws, reporting rules and evidence handling vary by law and hospital policy. Ask about principles (care first, document, preserve evidence), not legal citations.
Preset notes carry no verified doses. Items must not state drug doses unless the item is a calc with all numbers supplied.
Lab reference ranges vary by lab and source and several handout values are garbled. Ask about the priority action for an abnormal result, not the range.
